summary: A report on an Internet architecture workshop organized by the IAB and held at MCI in October 1994. It focused on aspects of the information infrastructure of the Internet.

plainLanguage.summary: The notes from a meeting where experts talked about how to find and share information on the Internet.

subtitle: Report from IAB workshop on Internet information architecture and infrastructure

tldr.problem: The Internet needed a coherent architecture for how information could be found, stored, cached, and accessed reliably as web and information services were becoming popular and experiencing scaling problems.
tldr.mechanism: An Internet Architecture Board workshop brought together 34 experts in October 1994 to discuss distributed caching, name resolution, security, and the components needed for a unified information infrastructure across the Internet.
tldr.outcome: The workshop produced three group reports recommending focus on caching and replication architecture, name resolution services, security frameworks, and a layered information architecture with core services.

facts.label: Breakout groups
facts.value: 3 groups addressing distributed databases, information architecture, and components

today: RFC 1862 is Informational and documents the state of thinking about Internet architecture in 1994. Its recommendations influenced the direction of work on HTTP caching, DNS extensions, and information services standards. The layered model and emphasis on caching and replication architecture proved prescient as web infrastructure became central to the Internet.

sections.title: The IAB Workshop on Information Infrastructure
sections.content:
In October 1994, the Internet Architecture Board held a workshop at MCI in Tysons Corner, Virginia to address long-term architectural issues for the Internet. The workshop brought together about 35 experts including IAB members, IETF Area Directors, and specialists in web technologies, naming, search, indexing, library services, and related fields.

The IAB, which provides strategic guidance on Internet development, holds these workshops to complement the ongoing engineering work of the IETF. The 1994 workshop focused specifically on the architecture of information applications and services on the Internet, aiming to provide the IETF with concrete recommendations and to improve communication between the communities working on different protocol layers.

Participants divided into three breakout groups that each produced a detailed report on their area of focus. This RFC compiles all three reports plus summary recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet's leaders got experts together to think about how the whole system should be organized for information services. They split up into groups to tackle different problems, then wrote down their ideas.

sections.title: Summary of Workshop Findings
sections.content:
Despite some disagreements on details, the three groups reached broad agreement on the general shape of an information architecture and its core principles. The workshop identified research needs and procedural recommendations for the IETF:

  • Research recommendations: Increased focus on general caching and replication architectures; rapid deployment of name resolution services; and articulation of a common security architecture for information applications.
  • Procedural recommendations: Making common identifiers and IANA-assigned numbers available in online databases; tightening security requirements on Proposed Standards; clarifying procedures for joining IETF working groups; and reviewing key distribution infrastructure for information applications.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone agreed on the big picture: the Internet needs better ways to copy information to different places, find things quickly, keep everything secure, and make the rules for how standards should work.

sections.title: Group 1: The Distributed Database Problem
sections.content:
The problem: Popular web and Gopher servers were experiencing serious overload from thousands of concurrent users. The DNS was being misused as a general-purpose replicated database because no better option existed, but it was not designed for that role.

Caching vs. replication: Group 1 distinguished two complementary approaches. Caching stores a partial set of data built on demand and is audience-specific. Replication stores the entire or a server-defined subset of data, pushed rather than pulled on demand, and can answer authoritatively about item existence. Both face common challenges around consistency and updates. Update strategies include master-slave, peer-to-peer, and flooding techniques (like NNTP), each with different consistency guarantees.

Management models: The group identified three approaches to organizing groups of cache and replication servers: a club model with minimal overhead, centrally coordinated service for optimized topology awareness, and hybrid combinations. A common management protocol would enable simplified control of distributed cache and replica servers.

Key recommendation: Define a general protocol for replicated databases and caching so different information applications can interoperate and be managed via a common interface.
sections.plainLanguage: When many people ask for the same popular website, the server gets overwhelmed. The group thought about two ways to fix it: keep copies nearby (caching), or have backup copies everywhere (replication). Both need careful management to keep copies up to date.

sections.title: Group 2A: Information Architecture Layers
sections.content:
Core model: Group 2A described an information architecture centered on objects (resources) with globally unique identifiers that are location-independent. Objects support one or more abstract types and exist at zero, one, or many locations simultaneously. The architecture also includes links expressing relationships among objects.

The wholesale layer: The group envisioned a layered model with an information 'wholesale' layer in the middle, providing general shared network-based information. Above sit 'retailers' (information providers to applications), and below are 'raw materials' (networking and operating system support).

Core services in the wholesale layer: Resource discovery (mapping descriptions to object identifiers), naming and identification, name/identification resolution, object retrieval, object publication, type definitions, attribute management, accounting and metering, pricing and billing, object storage and caching/replication, translation, server and service location, adaptive glue (quality of service negotiation), security services, and bootstrapping for new machines joining the infrastructure.

Key recommendation: Prioritize implementing object retrieval, name resolution, and caching/replication services first, as they are most immediately useful and actionable.
sections.plainLanguage: Information should be organized in layers. The middle layer should provide basic services like finding things, naming them, storing them, and keeping copies up to date. Applications sit above and the network sits below.

sections.title: Requirements from Lower Network Layers
sections.content:
Group 2A identified critical capabilities the lower network layers (raw materials) should provide to information services:

  • Connectivity information: Can the machine reach a local wire? A router? The global Internet? A specific host? Understanding connectivity is essential for adaptive behavior.
  • Bandwidth, latency, and reliability: Applications need to know available resources and ideally make reservations. The group ranked bandwidth, latency, and reliability (or a negotiated service envelope) as the second-highest priority for the lower layers.
  • Security constraints: Applications must be able to understand what security mechanisms are available. This ranked third in priority.
  • Cost information: If usage-based charging exists, applications need cost estimates.
  • Policy routing: Users should be able to identify their policy class for routing decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: The network layer needs to tell applications what resources are available: am I connected? How fast? How reliable? Can I afford this? This information helps applications make smart decisions.

sections.title: Group 2B: Information Architecture Components
sections.content:
Group 2B discussed practical components of an information architecture and addressed economic and philosophical questions about who bears costs for different services. The group examined specific topics including access and URLs, gateways between systems, URN resolution, type definitions and formats, service location and discovery, cache and replication, security and authentication, payments and charging, and presentation and search.

The group recognized that economic models matter: publishers naturally bear publishing costs and consumers bear consumption costs, but third-party services like translation are harder to justify economically.

All workshop groups emphasized that caching and replication are critical for scaling information services. They recognized that no single implementation can serve all needs—different situations require different strategies with varying consistency guarantees. The workshop concluded that defining a general protocol framework for distributed caching and replication would provide immediate benefits by enabling different implementations to interoperate and be managed uniformly. Such a framework could serve as a foundation for future protocols and improve existing ones.
sections.plainLanguage: The actual architecture needs to handle lots of practical details: finding things, understanding what type they are, keeping things secure, making copies, charging for services, and presenting information to users. The main takeaway is that Internet services need better ways to share and cache information reliably.
